extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, agency rulewriters, regulatory commenters, policy researchers tracking use of the "major questions" doctrine in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Register search-results listing showing documents that mention or rely on the "major questions" doctrine; useful for locating how agencies and courts invoke or respond to the doctrine across rulemakings. The page compiles excerpts and metadata from many agency actions referencing the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine — clear congressional authorization required
rubrics_metrics.description: “we lack the 'clear congressional authorization' required under the major questions doctrine” (quoted repeatedly across excerpts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine requires the government/agency to point to 'clear congressional authorization' before an agency may regulate on issues of major national significance. See West Virginia v. EPA and UARG cited in multiple excerpts. Guidance on application: courts will 'hesitate' to conclude Congress meant to confer authority on an agency for major questions and thus require explicit statutory text or clear delegation. Examples in the excerpts: EPA endangerment finding/GHG standards, OSHA vaccine-or-test, and other high-profile rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability threshold — 'vast' economic and political significance / major question
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine applies where the agency is asserting authority over a 'question of vast "economic and political significance"' or a 'major question of undeniable political and economic significance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agency action addresses matters of profound national consequence—e.g., national climate policy (Endangerment Finding/GHG vehicle standards), abortion policy, broad economic regulatory schemes—courts will analyze whether the action presents a 'major question.' The excerpts repeatedly characterize actions addressing global climate change, abortion, or nationwide employer-coverage rules as falling within this threshold. Agencies should assess whether the subject matter is reasonably described as 'major' before relying on broad statutory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency burden — identify and explain statutory authority when regulating on major questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies 'must identify clear statutory authority before regulating in areas of profound political consequence' and explain why the major questions doctrine does or does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency rule texts and responses to comments should point to explicit statutory provisions or clear congressional intent when asserting authority on major questions. If an agency contends the doctrine does not apply, it should explain why (see EPA's response to POLB comment #5 excerpt). Failure to explain or to cite clear authorization invites judicial skepticism and potential invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial consequences — invalidation or preliminary relief where clear authorization absent
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have invalidated or enjoined agency actions where the agency 'had exceeded its statutory authority' under the major questions doctrine (e.g., OSHA vaccine-or-test mandate; courts finding Non-Compete Rule violated the doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulewriters and commenters should treat invocation of the doctrine as a potential dispositive legal challenge: lack of clear authorization can lead to vacatur, rescission, or injunctions. The excerpts cite instances where district courts or higher courts concluded likely success on major-questions challenges or denied relief based on differing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by commenters — challenge agency authority on major-questions grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters routinely raise 'major questions' objections to agency proposals, arguing the agency lacks authority under the major questions doctrine (e.g., CFPB proposed registry, FTC Non-Compete Rule, other proposals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In notice-and-comment proceedings, expect stakeholders to question agencies' legal authority by invoking the doctrine. Agencies should anticipate and respond to such comments by articulating statutory bases and explaining why the doctrine does not preclude the action, or by providing clearer statutory support. The excerpts show agencies receiving and addressing such comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation/permissibility nuance — when delegations are acceptable with clear authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Some materials note that delegations to agencies to decide major policy questions may be permissible but only with clear congressional authorization or explicit delegation language (references to Order No. 1920, Paul v. U.S. (Kavanaugh statement)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and reviewers should analyze whether a statutory scheme contains sufficiently specific delegations that would allow an agency both to decide the major policy question and to regulate/enforce consequential choices. Courts may distinguish between permissible delegations (with clear authorization) and impermissible attempts to resolve major policy questions absent such clarity.
